sup-064316255265a882-0SL1q16:whole.hint: Measure the angles from the normal, and decide which medium the wave is entering.
notes: Use n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂. Frequency stays the same across a stationary boundary; speed and wavelength can change.
Total internal reflection requires travel from higher to lower refractive index and incidence above the critical angle, with sin θ_c = n₂/n₁.

duplicate-072d880c801aca4a.hint: Compare wave speeds on the two sides and draw a normal at the boundary.
notes: A wave entering a slower medium bends towards the normal; entering a faster medium bends away. Frequency stays fixed, so wavelength changes in proportion to speed.
Wavefronts are perpendicular to rays. For parallel faces returning to the original medium, the emerging ray is parallel to the incident ray but can be displaced sideways.

duplicate-49e98969ecfb49dc.hint: Check whether the question compares amplitude, intensity, or total power; these do not scale in the same way.
notes: For the same medium and frequency, intensity is proportional to amplitude squared. For an isotropic point source, I = P/(4πr²).
When coherent waves overlap, add their signed displacements first and then square the resultant amplitude. Adding intensities alone loses the interference effect.

duplicate-ebd59ebaefff6eeb.hint: Express the separation as a fraction of a complete wavelength or period.
notes: For a progressive sinusoidal wave, Δφ = 2πΔx/λ, or 2πΔt/T. A complete cycle is 2π radians, not π.
Account for any initial phase difference between the sources as well as the path difference. Equivalent phases differ by whole multiples of 2π.

duplicate-bc4dc021d4e3e48a.hint: Identify the boundary condition: must the end stay fixed, or can it move?
notes: A pulse reflecting from a fixed end is inverted; reflection from a free end is not. At a junction, distinguish reflected and transmitted pulses.
For reflection of light, incidence and reflection angles are measured from the normal. A plane-mirror image has the same perpendicular distance behind the mirror as the object has in front.

duplicate-a910fe6de27ffb6d.hint: Choose two well-separated points on the best-fit line, not necessarily two measured points.
notes: Gradient is the change in the vertical-axis quantity divided by the change in the horizontal-axis quantity. Here both axes are sines, so the gradient has no units.
Compare the plotted relation with Snell’s law to decide whether this gradient is the refractive-index ratio or its reciprocal.

duplicate-f8665b4d9b4fab78.hint: Write the required quantity in terms of the measurements, then track how each measurement’s uncertainty contributes.
notes: For products and quotients, add fractional uncertainties; for powers, multiply fractional uncertainty by the magnitude of the power. For sums and differences, combine absolute uncertainties using the stated worst-case convention.
For a graph gradient, use the steepest and shallowest acceptable lines through the error bars. Report an uncertainty with matching precision to the quantity, not extra calculator digits.
For the sketch, label both axes and show the correct intercepts, turning points and limiting behaviour. A qualitative sketch still needs the correct physical trend.

duplicate-4973d55a0d74b1b3.hint: Compare the wavelength with the opening or obstacle size.
notes: Diffraction becomes more pronounced when the wavelength is comparable with the aperture size. For a single slit, minima satisfy a sin θ = nλ for nonzero integer n.
The central maximum extends to the first minimum on both sides. Its full angular width is approximately 2λ/a at small angles, not λ/a.

duplicate-5649e7d68212acb0.hint: Compare the time spent in each region, not just the total path length.
notes: Travel time for each straight segment is distance divided by speed in that region. The quickest overall route can be longer if more of it lies in the faster region.
This is analogous to refraction: a path changes direction when the propagation speed changes across a boundary.

ibd-c0351bd864435118-q15:whole.hint: Move each wave to the same instant, then combine the displacements at each position.
notes: Superposition adds signed displacements, not speeds or frequencies. Opposite displacements can cancel while the waves continue to travel.
For pulses, first shift each shape by vt in its own travel direction, then add their heights point by point. After overlap, the original pulses continue unchanged in a linear medium.
